strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: online/continuous adaptation of interactive segmentation models using clinician clicks, which is important for real-world clinical deployment under distribution shift.

Proposed Gaussian Point Loss (GPL) is a simple, intuitive extension of sparse click-based losses to propagate supervision to a local neighborhood around clicks, addressing a clear limitation (sparsity) of prior methods (IA+SA, TSCA).

Two-stage adaptation (single-click localization stage + multi-click correction stage) is a reasonable design that separately targets segmentation quality and click-responsiveness, and ablations support the contribution of each component.

Extensive experimental evaluation across 9 databases (5 fundus, 4 brain MRI) spanning multiple types of distribution shift (inter-dataset shift, unseen modality, unseen pathology), which is more comprehensive than many related papers.

Method is compared against reasonable baselines (IA+SA, TSCA, MedSAM Adapter, frozen base model) and shows consistent improvements, including in low-click regimes and with fewer backpropagation steps than baselines, suggesting practical efficiency benefits.

Ablation study (Fig. 3) reasonably isolates the contribution of stage 1, stage 2, and GPL, and shows behavior over the image sequence (held-out test set), which helps validate the online-learning claim rather than just per-image performance.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: GPL is a straightforward Gaussian-weighted extension of standard cross-entropy near clicks, and the two-stage pseudo-label self-training strategy resembles existing self-training/pseudo-labeling online adaptation paradigms (e.g., TSCA's teacher-student framework); the paper does not strongly differentiate itself conceptually beyond removing extra regularizers.

The pseudo ground truth used for adaptation is the model's own prediction after T clicks, which is not necessarily equal to the true expert-corrected segmentation; the paper does not clearly justify why this self-generated label is trustworthy, especially under large distribution shift where predictions could be systematically biased or erroneous, potentially reinforcing model errors over time (error accumulation is only implicitly probed in the held-out curve in Fig. 3 bottom, which shows only 600 images and no variance/statistical significance).

Statistical significance is not reported for most tables (Tables 1-3); only Table 1 mentions averaging over 3 runs but no variance/std or significance tests are given for any of the comparisons, making it hard to judge robustness of reported gains, especially since some margins (e.g., GS1, GAMMA) are small.

Hyperparameters (α=0.7, β=200, σ=3, learning rates) appear to be fixed globally without justification or sensitivity analysis; given the claimed design goal of 'simplicity/robustness across distributions without technical oversight,' a hyperparameter sensitivity study would strengthen the practical claims but is missing.

The automatic click-simulation procedure (used both for training the base model and for generating online adaptation supervision) is a simplification of real user behavior; no experiments involve actual human-in-the-loop clicks or noisy/inconsistent real clinician interactions, which limits evidence for real-world applicability despite motivating the paper via clinical workflows.

Method description of Stage 2's generated correction-click sampling and connected-component-based click generation lacks full detail/formalization (e.g., how many points are generated, randomness control, reproducibility of click generation algorithm), somewhat limiting reproducibility together with the promise to release code only 'upon publication.'

The evaluation is restricted to 2D slice segmentation for brain MRI (single largest-lesion slice, merged into one class), which is a substantial simplification relative to real volumetric clinical segmentation tasks and may overstate generalizability to full 3D clinical use.

Only limited backbone comparison (ISFCNN-based CNN) is explored; no evaluation with transformer-based interactive backbones (e.g., SAM-family models beyond MedSAM Adapter as baseline) integrated with the proposed adaptation strategy, leaving open whether GPL/two-stage adaptation generalizes to other architectures.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: adapting interactive segmentation models to post-deployment distribution shift using click feedback.
Broad experimental coverage across 9 databases (5 fundus, 4 brain MRI) and multiple types of shift (inter-dataset, modality, pathology).
The two-stage design (localization-click fine-tuning + correction-click fine-tuning with GPL) is simple and computationally cheap relative to baselines (fewer backprop steps than TSCA/IA+SA).
Ablation study (Fig. 3) isolates the contribution of Stage 1, Stage 2, and GPL, showing each component contributes to final performance and to stability over the adaptation sequence.
Consistent, sometimes large, quantitative improvements over TSCA and IA+SA baselines across most reported settings.
weaknesses: The central premise—'learning from user interaction'—is not actually validated with real user corrections. The 'pseudo ground truth' used for adaptation is the base model's own prediction after simulated automatic clicks (generated via connected-component error analysis on the dataset's own labels), not genuine independent clinician feedback. This makes the adaptation loop largely self-distillation on synthetic clicks, which risks reinforcing systematic model biases and overstates the claim of learning from 'user interaction' in a realistic clinical sense.

No real user study or qualitative analysis of behavior with actual noisy/inconsistent human clicks; all reported experiments rely on synthetic, deterministic click simulation, which may not reflect real interactive workflows (click placement variability, fatigue, mistakes).

Limited baseline comparison: only IA+SA, TSCA, and (in one experiment) a SAM adapter are compared; no comparison against more recent/foundation-model-based interactive segmentation or test-time adaptation methods, limiting claims of state-of-the-art status.

Technical novelty is incremental—the Gaussian Point Loss is essentially a spatially-weighted cross-entropy loss around click locations, and the two-stage pseudo-label fine-tuning scheme closely resembles standard self-training/pseudo-labeling strategies already used in prior interactive-adaptation works (e.g., TSCA's teacher-student framework).

Key hyperparameters (β=200, σ=3, learning rates) appear hand-tuned per modality without sensitivity analysis, undermining the paper's claimed 'simplicity/robustness for deployment without expert oversight.'
No variance/statistical significance reporting despite averaging over 3 runs in some tables; gains in several settings (e.g., GS1, GAMMA) are small and could be within noise.

Brain MRI evaluation is restricted to a single 2D slice per case (largest lesion area), which is a significant simplification relative to realistic 3D clinical segmentation workflows, limiting clinical relevance of the reported gains.

The risk of error accumulation/drift during continuous online adaptation (since pseudo-GT is model-generated) is only partially examined (Fig. 3 bottom panel on a held-out split of one dataset); no broader analysis of long-term stability, catastrophic drift, or failure modes across the full range of datasets.
Figure 2 results are described only qualitatively ('maintains trends') without a quantitative table, weakening the evidentiary support for claims about combined modality+pathology shift robustness.

strengths: Addresses a practical and clinically-relevant problem: continuously adapting interactive segmentation models using naturally-occurring user corrections after deployment, without requiring extra annotation effort.

The Gaussian Point Loss is a sensible and well-motivated fix to the sparse-click supervision problem in prior online adaptation methods (IA+SA, TSCA), propagating confidence around clicks via a Gaussian weighting instead of relying only on the clicked pixel plus extra regularizers.

Broad and diverse experimental evaluation: 5 fundus datasets and 4 brain MRI datasets, covering multiple realistic distribution-shift scenarios (cross-dataset, cross-modality, cross-pathology, combined shifts), which strengthens the generality claims.

Consistent, sizeable improvements over both a frozen base model and two continual-adaptation baselines (IA+SA, TSCA) across nearly all settings and click counts (1/5/10 clicks), including favorable results with fewer clicks (3-click experiment).

Efficiency argument is credible and practically important: the method reaches strong performance with only two backpropagation passes per image versus 10+ for baselines, which matters for real-time clinical usage.

Reasonably thorough ablation study (Fig. 3) isolating the contributions of Stage 1, Stage 2, and GPL, including a sequential/streaming evaluation on held-out images showing the full method's advantage grows over time rather than just at a single snapshot.
weaknesses: The base interactive model (ISFCNN, a 2019 CNN with click channels) is relatively dated; modern SAM-style backbones are only used as a separate baseline (MedSAM Adapter) rather than being tested within the proposed adaptation framework, leaving open whether gains transfer to stronger/more modern architectures.

Brain MRI evaluation is restricted to single 2D slices (largest-lesion slice) with all lesion labels merged into one class, which simplifies the task considerably relative to real clinical 3D multi-class segmentation and limits the strength of the distribution-shift claims.

Limited statistical rigor: although TSCA/OAIMS results are said to be averaged over three runs, no variance/standard deviation or significance testing is reported in the tables, making it hard to assess whether some of the reported gains (particularly smaller ones on GS1/GAMMA) are meaningful.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental — the method largely combines existing components (pseudo-label self-training, Dice-Focal loss, two-stage fine-tuning, a locally-weighted click loss) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper explicitly frames this as a virtue ("simplicity"), but reviewers focused on novelty may see this as limited.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is not explored: the fixed 11x11 window and σ=3 in GPL, as well as β=200 weighting, are set without ablation or discussion of how they generalize across different image resolutions/anatomies (fundus vs. brain MRI use the same values despite very different image scales).

The click-simulation protocol (fixed T=10 corrective clicks per image, same automated point-generation heuristic used for training, adaptation, and evaluation) is somewhat idealized and may not capture realistic variability in real clinician click behavior, so real-world applicability is not directly validated with human-in-the-loop experiments.

One dataset (TBI) is a private institutional dataset, which limits reproducibility of a subset of the experiments; code/models are only promised "upon publication," so reproducibility cannot currently be verified.

The footnoted exclusion of catastrophic forgetting from the scope is reasonable but under-discussed; in real deployment, continual online updates without any forgetting mitigation could be a practical concern the paper does not empirically probe (e.g., performance drift on the original training distribution over long adaptation sequences).

strengths: Extensive experimental validation across 9 diverse databases (5 fundus, 4 brain-MRI) and multiple types of distribution shift (cross-scanner, cross-modality, cross-pathology), providing strong empirical support for the method's generality.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (CCG loss in pretraining/PI/MI, Gaussian vs. uniform kernel, class-restriction mechanism, hyperparameters α, β, σ), which clarifies design choices.

Practical, lean design with negligible computational latency (sub-second even on CPU), making the method plausible for real clinical deployment, and requiring far fewer gradient updates than prior online-adaptation baselines.

Careful robustness analysis: resilience to noisy/wrong user clicks, worst-case-first image ordering, extreme domain shift, and overfitting under large click budgets — addressing legitimate concerns about pseudo-label error accumulation.

Comparison against relevant unsupervised-adaptation baselines (entropy minimization, plain cross-entropy self-training) convincingly shows that naive pseudo-labeling is insufficient, supporting the necessity of the click-centered design.
Additional useful analyses such as number of clicks needed to reach target Dice, and behavior on source-like (no-shift) data, which strengthen the practical relevance of the claims.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core ideas (using corrected predictions as pseudo ground-truth for self-training, spatially-weighted click losses) build closely on existing self-training/pseudo-labeling and click-based interactive segmentation literature; the main contribution is a targeted combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Backbone is restricted to a single U-Net; the claim that the method is "model-agnostic" is not empirically validated with alternative architectures (e.g., transformer-based SAM-style backbones), which would strengthen generality claims given SAM/MedSAM are cited as motivating context.

Evaluation is done on 2D slices selected as the largest-lesion slice from 3D MRI volumes, which simplifies the problem and may not reflect realistic clinical interactive segmentation workflows on full volumes.

All experiments rely on simulated user clicks (including error simulation), not real clinician interaction studies; actual human click behavior, timing, and error patterns could differ substantially from the synthetic click-generation heuristics used.

The overall pipeline includes many interacting components and hyperparameters (α, β, σ, two-stage PI, per-click MI, CCG loss design choices), which somewhat undercuts the claimed simplicity/'lean' advantage over baselines that need extra regularizers.
One of the four MRI datasets (TBI) is private, limiting full reproducibility of a subset of results despite promise to release code/pretrained models.

Baseline comparisons could be questioned: Med-SA performs surprisingly poorly across the board, and IA+SA/TSCA were reimplemented by the authors rather than using original released checkpoints, leaving some uncertainty about implementation fidelity.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 9 databases (5 fundus, 4 brain-MRI) covering multiple types of distribution shift: cross-database, cross-modality, and cross-pathology.

Thorough ablation studies dissecting the contribution of each loss term (DF/CCG) in both Post-Interaction and Mid-Interaction stages, as well as hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (alpha, beta, sigma).

Multiple robustness analyses are included: overfitting under a large click budget, robustness to 'worst-case-first' image ordering, robustness to noisy/incorrect user clicks, and re-adaptation after a distribution shift returns to source domain.

Comparison against relevant baselines (IA+SA, TSCA, Med-SA/SAM-based adapter) and against simple unsupervised alternatives (pseudo-label cross-entropy, entropy minimization), which helps justify the specific design choices (CCG loss, click-centered weighting) rather than generic self-training.
Reported computational latency is negligible even on CPU, supporting the claimed practicality for real-time clinical workflows.
Clear algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1 and 2) and reasonably detailed method exposition aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on simulated clicks rather than real human/clinician interaction; for a method centered on 'clinician guidance,' the complete absence of a real user study is a significant gap that limits confidence in real-world applicability and click-quality/pseudo-label-quality assumptions.

Although the target data (brain MRI, in particular) are inherently 3D volumes, evaluation is restricted to a single 2D slice per case (the one with the largest lesion), which is a considerable simplification that avoids the harder and more clinically relevant 3D interactive segmentation setting.

The method is framed as 'lean' and 'practical,' yet it involves a fairly complex pipeline (two-stage Post-Interaction adaptation, Mid-Interaction adaptation, CCG loss with several hyperparameters sigma/alpha/beta) that partially undercuts this claim; hyperparameters were tuned in preliminary experiments and then fixed globally, but sensitivity plots (e.g., sigma=0 instability) suggest the method is not trivially robust to poor tuning.

The Med-SA (SAM-based) baseline performs substantially worse than the simple U-Net backbone across nearly all settings, which is somewhat counter to typical findings in the interactive segmentation literature and raises questions about whether the SAM-based baseline was adequately tuned/fine-tuned for a fair comparison.

Core novelty is somewhat incremental: the main technical contributions (using post-correction predictions as pseudo-ground-truth, and a Gaussian-weighted click-centered loss) are natural combinations of existing ideas (pseudo-labeling/self-training, online learning for interactive segmentation, distance-weighted loss functions) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

No statistical significance testing (confidence intervals/variance across seeds) is reported for the main results tables (Tables 1-4), aside from a single 3-seed variance check in one ablation, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements over TSCA/IA+SA are robust or within noise, especially for smaller gaps (e.g., GS1, GAMMA).

The framework's core assumption -- that user-corrected final masks are 'good enough' as pseudo-ground-truth -- is only partially stress-tested; for genuinely difficult distribution shifts, users themselves may struggle to correct systematically wrong model outputs (e.g., structures the model cannot even partially localize), and this scenario is only lightly explored via the extreme-shift ATLAS experiment.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: leveraging interactive segmentation's user feedback loop specifically for online adaptation to distribution shift in medical imaging, a natural but underexplored synergy.

The proposed Click-Centered Gaussian (CCG) loss is simple, well-justified (class-restricted, Gaussian-weighted around clicks) and shown to be broadly useful across pretraining, Mid-Interaction, and Post-Interaction stages via careful ablations.

Very extensive experimental validation: 5 fundus and 4 brain-MRI databases, multiple types of distribution shift (cross-scanner, cross-modality, cross-pathology), and consistent improvements over strong baselines (IA+SA, TSCA, Med-SA/SAM-based).

Thorough ablation and robustness studies in the appendix are a real strength: hyperparameter sensitivity (α, β, σ), overfitting under large click budgets, robustness to noisy/incorrect user clicks, robustness to 'worst-case-first' image ordering, performance on source-like data (no degradation), and comparison against alternative unsupervised objectives (entropy minimization, plain cross-entropy pseudo-labeling) showing the CCG-based approach is not simply exploiting pseudo-labeling per se.

Practical considerations are addressed: negligible computational latency (even on CPU), clicks-to-target-Dice efficiency analysis, and a method that needs no additional regularizers unlike prior online adaptation approaches.
The two-stage Post-Interaction/Mid-Interaction decomposition is intuitive and each component's incremental contribution is empirically demonstrated (Tables 5, 6, 13).
weaknesses: All experiments rely on simulated user clicks (heuristic largest-error-region click placement) rather than real clinician interactions; no user study validates that real annotators would produce the same quality corrections or interaction patterns assumed by the pseudo-ground-truth mechanism.

3D MRI volumes are evaluated only via a single 2D slice per case (largest lesion slice), which simplifies the problem and may not reflect realistic clinical interactive segmentation workflows for volumetric data.

The method introduces several hyperparameters (α, β, σ) that, while shown to be relatively robust, still require tuning; the pipeline (two-stage PI + per-click MI) is somewhat complex, and the true end-to-end benefit versus a simpler single-stage adaptation isn't isolated (S1PI and S2PI conflated into pipeline necessity without a from-scratch alternative baseline design).

The Med-SA/SAM-based comparison is not entirely fair as a baseline since it is frozen at test time while all other compared methods perform online adaptation, making the comparison more illustrative than a rigorous ablation of transformer backbones under the same adaptation scheme.

Backbone is restricted to a single U-Net architecture; despite claims of model-agnosticism, no experiments validate the framework with a transformer/SAM-style backbone combined with the proposed online adaptation, leaving this claim untested.

Most main-table results appear to be single-run point estimates without confidence intervals or multiple seeds (only a subset of ablations in the appendix use 3 seeds), limiting statistical confidence in the reported gains, especially for smaller distribution shifts (e.g., GS1, GAMMA) where margins are narrow.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the individual components (Gaussian-weighted click loss, pseudo-label based online adaptation, teacher-student style updates) build closely on established ideas (e.g., TSCA, IA+SA, entropy minimization/pseudo-labeling), with the main contribution being a careful combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
